items.title: RAG vs. retriever-free RAG, clearly explained!
items.summary:
RAG vs. retriever-free RAG, clearly explained!

(powered by decision models like Jev)

In a standard RAG setup, documents are split into chunks, converted into embeddings, and stored in a vector index.

When a query arrives, the system embeds it and pulls the top-k chunks with the closest vectors.

A reranker then reorders those candidates against the query, and the best few go to the LLM as context.

The problem is that the similarity search decides what the LLM can ever see.

If the right passage never made the top-k, nothing later in the pipeline can bring it back, not even a strong reranker.

Retriever-free RAG, from a new Cornell and ASAPP paper, keeps the documents and the LLM but replaces similarity search with navigation.

The documents are organized as a document tree, like a table of contents, and a decision model (Jev 1.13) walks down it.

A decision model doesn't generate text. It reads one shared context and returns a probability for every yes/no question about it, in one forward pass per stage.

Here's how a query moves through the tree:

↳ Top documents: the model reads the query beside every candidate document, asks "Is this relevant?" for each, and keeps the best few.
↳ Top passages: it opens only those documents and asks the same question for every passage inside them.
↳ Most relevant? (optional): a single multiple-choice question reorders the top 20 passages (top 5 on Natural Questions).

Dropped documents are never opened, so their passages are never scored.

On Natural Questions (2.68M Wikipedia paragraphs), its top pick contained the answer 65.4% of the time. Embedding search plus an 8B reranker got 48.0%, and GPT-5 reranking got 60.8%.

The gain comes from ranking, not coverage. Embedding search's top 100 holds the answer more often than the navigated shortlist (98.4% vs 94.0%), but navigation is better at putting it first.

Median retrieval takes under 2 seconds per query, but each method was timed in a different setup, so it isn't a controlled speed comparison.

The main limit is that it needs a sensible hierarchy, and a document pruned early is gone for good. It also skips embedding search only at query time, since the Wikipedia tree was built offline using embeddings.

The diagram below depicts the complete flow.

- RAG retrieves by similarity, then reranks.
- Retriever-free RAG navigates a document tree with a decision model.
- The LLM answers from the top passages.

If you're building a RAG system, this is worth benchmarking against your current setup.

Here's the paper: https://t.co/U7cCcIfZV1

If you're new to decision models, I've quoted my full breakdown of how Jev works below.

items.title: 【ChatGPT 擦边技巧汇总】
items.summary:
【ChatGPT 擦边技巧汇总】

GPT现在作图依然独一档强大，甚至擦边方面还挺宽容的
但是最近留言区有人说我的图根本不是GPT出的，都是骗人的
那我干脆教给大家技巧吧：

1、抽卡
是哦，这要抽卡的，在大量被平台屏蔽的过程中抽卡，优质提示词可以提高抽卡概率，降低抽卡难度，但你可别指望都能随便出，一次被挡住，不代表不能出
我一般用“命中率”给每次的提示词加个出图概率，20%指平均每5次出一次图

2、垫图
垫图的话，出擦边的概率是要下降一层的，审核更加敏感一些，尤其注意不要垫的图都很敏感，更麻烦了
有些图怎么也出不来，尝试文生图试试吧
不过呢，这倒没有特别关键

3、修图
很好用的模式，特别适合当某张图出来后整体还不错，但细节有瑕疵的情况哦
你只需要点开这张图，在想优化的位置点击“评论”，加上优化指令，一次能加多个，重新修一下图
这里注意，还是要抽卡！如果被屏蔽了，多试几次吧，很重要的技巧哦！

4、空间限制
技术层面来说，越复杂的动作，越容易出现各种扭曲问题，空间位置不垫图说明，文字驱动非常困难
喜欢纯文生图，更像一种手活儿情结吧，实数没有太大必要，目标是出图的话，多模态更好，参考图生图
不过，肢体动作参考图，远没有大家以为的好用，死板不灵活

5、合理理由
AI可以被绕过机制的重大技巧之一，给它语境，令它有充分理由出图
说自己在进行艺术创作，医学研究这类理由，就能提高出好卡的概率，真的有用

6、举一反三
作图嘛，最舒服的还是多刷别人的创意，自己举一反三的改元素，我之前做的雕塑风格擦边，有高手给上色，做群像，超有趣，大家这样才对嘛

items.title: 8 AI model architectures, visually explained:
items.summary:
8 AI model architectures, visually explained:

LLMs get so much attention that it's easy to overlook the rest of the field. Different inputs, tasks, and deployment constraints have led to very different model designs.

Here are eight specialized AI model architectures:

1. LLM (Large language models)

Text is split into tokens, mapped to embeddings, and processed through transformer layers. The model generates its response by predicting successive tokens.

↳ GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama.

2. LCM (Large concept models)

Moves prediction to the sentence level. Sentences become SONAR embeddings, and the model predicts the next sentence representation. Meta explored both autoregressive and diffusion-based versions.

↳ Meta's LCM research introduced this approach.

3. LAM (Large action models)

Connects a user's request to actions in an environment. These systems interpret intent, plan steps, and use interfaces or tools, often checking results before continuing.

↳ Rabbit R1, Microsoft UFO, Claude Computer Use.

4. MoE (Mixture of experts)

A router assigns token representations to selected expert networks inside the model. Activating a subset of experts adds model capacity without running every expert for every token.

↳ Mixtral, DeepSeek, Switch Transformer.

5. VLM (Vision-language models)

Combines visual representations with language processing. A vision encoder extracts image features, which are connected to a language model so it can answer questions about visual content.

↳ GPT-4V, Gemini, LLaVA.

6. SLM (Small language models)

Uses fewer parameters to reduce memory and compute requirements. These models can run locally, with quantization often reducing their deployment footprint further.

↳ Phi-3, Gemma, Mistral 7B, Llama 3.2 1B.

7. MLM (Masked language models)

Learns by predicting hidden tokens using context on both sides. This bidirectional training produces representations useful for retrieval, classification, and other language-understanding tasks.

↳ BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa.

8. SAM (Segment Anything Model)

An image encoder processes the image, while a prompt encoder handles points, boxes, or masks. A mask decoder combines them to identify the requested regions.

↳ Meta's SAM supports interactive segmentation and image annotation.

These aren't eight mutually exclusive categories. A small model can process images, and a language model can use MoE layers. Some labels describe architecture, while others describe training or intended use.

There's another approach I kept outside the image because it alters how a model handles context rather than introducing a separate model family.

Recursive language models, from MIT, put the input into a Python environment that a root model can inspect through code.

The model can search or slice that input, then make recursive model calls on selected portions instead of loading everything into its own context window.

The reported experiments handled inputs beyond 10 million tokens without retraining, with gains over the base model even on some tasks whose inputs already fit its context window.

I recently wrote a full breakdown of how this works, including why accessing a large input and reasoning reliably over it are different problems.

Read it below.

result.actual_text:
Nguyên hàm của \(x^2\) là:

\[
\int x^2\,dx = \frac{x^3}{3} + C
\]

với \(C\) là hằng số tích phân.

**Kiểm tra lại:** đạo hàm của \(\frac{x^3}{3}\) là \(\frac{3x^2}{3} = x^2\) ✓

items.title: Exclusive: OpenAI targets Microsoft's GitHub with deal
items.summary:
OpenAI will acquire Pierre Computer, a developer tools startup whose technology is already embedded in Codex, the company told Axios exclusively.

Why it matters:OpenAI is joining a slew of companies challenging Microsoft's GitHub as AI agents take on more coding work. The platform has acted as a central repository and nerve center for software development for many years.

Zoom out:GitHub has faced a number of reliability issues and outages as AI coding has taken off. [...] Financial terms were not disclosed. Pierre's open-source projects will remain open-source.

Between the lines:Earlier this week, OpenAI revealed Pando, built to handle the explosion of code generated by AI agents.

   OpenAI says Pando reduced the time needed to push code changes by nearly 80%. 
   The company is now exploring ways to make the technology available to customers. [...] Cursor, now owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, launched GitHub rival Origin in August.
   Former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke, who launched a new coding startup, announced a competing product last month.
   Microsoft owns nearly a quarter of OpenAI, although the two companies also compete in a variety of ways, a dynamic that is common across the competitive AI landscape.

Driving the news: OpenAI plans to integrate Pierre's Code Storage function into Codex, where Pierre's technology is already used.
